name: read_file
description:
Reads the contents of a file — or of many files in one call — from the local filesystem, handling text, image, notebook, and other binary files appropriately.
Pass an ARRAY of absolute paths and/or glob patterns (or one glob pattern) to read many files in a single call: their contents come back concatenated under "// File: <path> (<type>)" headers, after a "Read X/Y files" summary and any per-file errors. Multi-file reads skip node_modules, build output and .gitignored files by default, extract documents, note other binary files instead of inlining them, and ignore offset/limit.
Text content is returned with each line prefixed by its 1-indexed line number as "<line>: <content>" (a file containing "foo" comes back as "1: foo"). The prefix is for reference only — never include it when quoting file content or when building edit_file old_string/new_string values.
Pass a negative offset to count back from the end: offset=-50 returns the last 50 lines, so the tail of a log needs one call rather than a length-finding read followed by a second read.
By default up to 2000 lines are returned from the start of the file; output is also capped at 128 KB and any single line longer than 2000 characters is truncated with a marker. When a read is truncated, a note states the exact offset to continue from — prefer one larger window over many tiny repeated slices, and use the grep tool instead to find specific content in large files.
Image files (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .bmp, .tiff) are shown directly to vision-capable models: read an image to actually see its contents, the same as if it had been attached — screenshots included. Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) are returned as tagged cells with their outputs (plots attached as images) instead of raw JSON. Documents (.pdf, .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, .odt, .ods, .odp, .rtf, .epub and their legacy .doc/.ppt/.xls forms) are extracted to Markdown with headings, tables and lists preserved, windowed by offset/limit (negative offset for the tail) like any text read; a PDF with no text layer says so and tells you how to view its pages instead of returning nothing. The first document read on a machine fetches the converter into the user cache (one npm install, needs network); later reads reuse it. SVG files are read as text. Other binary files return their file type without loading the binary into memory.
Re-reading the same window of an unchanged file returns a short "file unchanged" note instead of the content — the earlier read in this conversation is still current. An empty file returns an explicit note, as does an offset beyond the end of the file.
The tool validates that the provided path is absolute, inside the workspace, and points to an existing readable file; if the file is missing it retries macOS filename spelling variants and suggests similarly named siblings. Device/stream paths like /dev/stdin are refused.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to read. Must be a complete path starting from the root directory (/ on Unix/Linux/macOS or C:\ on Windows). The path must be inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories). May also be a single glob pattern, which reads every match. To read several files at once, use `paths` instead.

paths.description: Read MANY files in one call: absolute paths and/or glob patterns, e.g. ["/repo/src/index.ts", "/repo/src/**/*.test.ts"]. Use this instead of file_path (not alongside it) when you need more than one file; a pattern without a leading / resolves against target_directory.

offset.description: The 1-indexed line number to start reading from (the first line is 1). Omit to read from the start of the file. Truncation notes in the output state the exact offset to continue with when a file needs more than one read. A NEGATIVE offset counts back from the END of the file: offset=-50 starts 50 lines before the end, so offset=-50 alone returns the last 50 lines, and offset=-50 with limit=10 returns the first 10 of those. Use it to inspect the tail of a log or an append-only file without first reading it to learn how long it is.

limit.description: The maximum number of lines to read starting from offset. Must be a positive integer. Defaults to 2000 lines.

exclude.description: Multi-file reads: glob patterns to skip, e.g. ["**/*.test.ts"].

target_directory.description: Multi-file reads: base directory for relative patterns (default: the current directory, and must be inside the workspace).

default_exclude.description: Multi-file reads: set false to stop skipping node_modules, dist, build, coverage and other build artifacts (default true).

git_ignore.description: Multi-file reads: set false to stop skipping .gitignored files (default true).

name: write_file
description:
Creates or overwrites a file with the specified content at the given absolute path, automatically creating any necessary parent directories.
If the file already exists it will be completely overwritten with the new content, so you MUST read the file (with read_file) before writing to it: overwriting a file that has not been read in this session is rejected, as is overwriting a file that changed on disk after it was last read, and a partial read (offset/limit window or truncated preview) does not count as having read it.
Writes are atomic (a unique temporary sibling is written and renamed into place), an existing symlink is preserved and its target replaced, existing file permissions are kept, and a UTF-16LE or BOM-prefixed file keeps its original encoding.
Prefer edit_file for targeted changes to an existing file; use this tool to create new files or intentionally replace a file's full content.
All new content is written as UTF-8 encoded text (unless preserving an existing file's encoding), making it suitable for source code, configuration files, documentation, and other text-based formats. Line endings are written exactly as supplied.

file_path.description: The absolute path where the file should be written. Must be a complete path starting from the root directory (/ on Unix/Linux/macOS or C:\ on Windows). The path must be inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories). If parent directories do not exist, they will be created automatically. An existing file at this path must have been read with read_file before it can be overwritten.

content.description: The text content to write to the file. Can be any UTF-8 string including multi-line text, JSON, XML, source code, or any other text format. Empty strings are valid and will create an empty file. Line endings are preserved as provided.

name: edit_file
description:
Performs precise text replacements in files by finding and replacing exact string matches, similar to a str_replace operation.
The old_string should match the file contents exactly; when it does not, the tool falls back to increasingly lenient matching (smart quotes/dashes, per-line whitespace, indentation shifts, block anchors) and reports which strategy matched, so minor copy differences do not fail the edit.
By default old_string must identify a UNIQUE location: if it matches more than once the edit is rejected with the match count — add more surrounding context to disambiguate, set replace_all to true to change every occurrence, or set replacement_count to replace the first N occurrences explicitly.
An empty old_string creates the file: if the file does not exist it is created with new_string as its content (parent directories are created automatically); if it exists and is non-empty the edit is rejected.
If the file changed on disk after it was last read in this session, the edit is rejected until the file is read again, so external changes are never silently overwritten.
The file's byte-order mark and line endings (LF or CRLF) are preserved exactly, writes are atomic (temp file + rename through any symlink, preserving the file mode), and the result includes a line-numbered snippet of the edited region for verification.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to edit (a leading ~/ is expanded to the home directory). Must be a complete path starting from the root directory (/ on Unix/Linux/macOS or C:\ on Windows). The path must be inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories). Binary files cannot be edited with this tool.

old_string.description: The exact text to search for, including whitespace, indentation and line breaks. Must identify a unique location unless replace_all or replacement_count is set. Pass an empty string to create a new file (with new_string as its content) when the file does not exist.

new_string.description: The replacement text inserted in place of each matched occurrence of old_string. Must differ from old_string. Can be an empty string to delete the matched text (deleting a whole line also removes its trailing newline).

replace_all.description: When true, replaces ALL occurrences of old_string in the file. Use for renames that repeat through a file. When false (default), old_string must match exactly once.

replacement_count.description: Explicitly replace the first N occurrences (scanning from the top of the file). Must be a positive integer no greater than the number of occurrences. Only needed for deliberate partial replacements; prefer a unique old_string or replace_all.

name: read_directory
description:
Lists the contents of a directory, providing separate arrays of files and subdirectories found at the specified path.
This tool is essential for exploring project structure, discovering available files, and understanding directory organization before performing operations on specific files.
It automatically respects .gitignore patterns by default when operating within git repositories, ensuring you don't see files that are intentionally excluded from version control.
The tool supports custom exclusion patterns using glob syntax, allowing you to filter out specific files or directories based on your needs, such as build artifacts or temporary files.
Results are always sorted alphabetically for consistent output, making it easier to locate specific items in large directories.
It should be used when you need to explore a directory's contents, verify file existence, or understand project structure before performing file operations.

path.description: The absolute path to the directory to read. Must be a complete path starting from the root directory (/ on Unix/Linux/macOS or C:\ on Windows). The path must be inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories). The directory must exist and be accessible. Returns an error if the path points to a file instead of a directory.

exclude.description: Optional array of glob patterns to exclude from results. Uses minimatch syntax for pattern matching. Examples: ["*.log", "temp*", "**/*.tmp"] would exclude all log files, anything starting with "temp", and all .tmp files in any subdirectory. Patterns are applied in addition to any .gitignore rules.

name: glob
description:
Fast file-pattern matching tool that works with codebases of any size, returning file paths that match a glob pattern sorted by modification time (most recently changed first).
This tool matches file paths against glob patterns such as **/*.js or src/**/*.ts, making it ideal for locating files by name, extension, or directory structure without inspecting file contents. Absolute patterns like /repo/src/**/*.ts are supported directly — the static directory prefix becomes the search root.
Results are paginated: by default the first 100 matches are returned and a truncation notice is appended when more exist; use limit and offset to page through large result sets, or narrow the pattern.
Hidden (dot) files and gitignored files are searched by default (.git internals never are); set COMMAND_CODE_GLOB_HIDDEN=0 or COMMAND_CODE_GLOB_NO_IGNORE=0 in the environment to exclude hidden files or respect ignore rules (gitignore plus common build/cache directories such as node_modules, dist, coverage).
It should be used when you need to find files by naming or path patterns, explore the structure of an unfamiliar codebase, locate configuration or entry-point files, or prepare a targeted set of files for further inspection with tools like grep. When doing an open-ended exploration that may require multiple rounds of globbing and content-searching, use the agent/task tool instead.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match files. Supports wildcards: * matches any characters except /, ** matches any characters including / (for recursive search), ? matches single character, [abc] matches character set, {js,ts} matches alternatives. Examples: "**/*.ts" finds all TypeScript files recursively, "src/**/*.{js,jsx}" finds JavaScript files in src directory, "*.json" finds JSON files in the search directory. Absolute patterns like "/repo/packages/**/config-*" are also supported.

path.description: Optional directory to search in. Accepts a path relative to the current working directory, an absolute path, or a ~-prefixed home path. The path must resolve inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories), must exist, and must be a directory. Omit it (do NOT pass "" or sentinel strings like "undefined") to search the current working directory.

limit.description: Optional maximum number of results to return (default 100). Must be a positive integer. Results beyond the limit produce a truncation notice with the total match count.

offset.description: Optional number of matches to skip before returning results (default 0), for paginating past the first page. Matches are ordered by modification time, most recent first.

name: grep
description:
A powerful search tool built on ripgrep

Usage:
- ALWAYS use this grep tool for search tasks. NEVER invoke `grep` or `rg` as a shell command. This tool is optimized for correct permissions and access.
- Supports full regular-expression syntax, for example "log.*Error" or "function\s+\w+"
- Filter paths with the glob parameter, for example "**/tests/**" or "*.{ts,tsx}", or the type parameter, for example "js", "py", or "rust"
- Output modes: "content" shows matching lines, "files_with_matches" shows only matching paths and is the default, and "count" shows match counts per file
- Results are paginated with head_limit (default 250 rows) and offset; pass head_limit: 0 for unlimited
- Pattern syntax uses ripgrep, not grep. Literal braces need escaping; use `interface\{\}` to find `interface{}` in Go code.
- Patterns match within one line by default. For cross-line patterns such as `struct \{[\s\S]*?field`, use `multiline: true`.

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search in. Must resolve inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories). Defaults to the current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern(s) to filter files, for example "*.js" or "*.{ts,tsx}". Multiple patterns may be separated by spaces or commas; brace alternatives are preserved.

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (default), "count" shows match counts per file.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match. Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match. Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-C.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match. Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Alias for -C; takes precedence over -C when both are set. Requires output_mode: "content".

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (default true). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

type.description: File type to search, for example "js", "py", "rust". More efficient than glob for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to the first N lines/entries (default 250). Works in all output modes. Pass 0 for unlimited.

offset.description: Skip the first N lines/entries before applying head_limit (default 0). Works in all output modes.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (default false).

name: shell_command
description:
Executes shell commands in a controlled environment with comprehensive output capture, timeout protection, and working directory management, enabling system operations, build processes, and tool integrations.
This tool spawns commands as child processes with full control over execution environment, capturing both standard output and error streams while monitoring exit codes and signals, making it ideal for running build scripts, executing CLI tools, performing system operations, or integrating with external programs.
Commands run with shell interpretation enabled for cross-platform compatibility, supporting pipes, redirections, and shell built-ins, with automatic timeout termination to prevent hanging processes from blocking execution.
When a command should keep running, such as a dev server, watcher, or long-running local service, set run_in_background=true. Background commands return immediately with a task id, PID, cwd, and output log path, then can be inspected with shell_tasks or stopped with kill_shell by taskId.
The tool provides detailed execution results including stdout, stderr, exit codes, and execution duration, helping diagnose issues and verify successful completion of operations. Conventional non-error exit codes are annotated (grep/rg exit 1 means "no matches found", diff/cmp exit 1 means "files differ", test exit 1 means "condition is false") so they are not mistaken for failures.
Very large output is truncated middle-out: the head and tail are kept inline and the FULL output is saved to a log file whose path is included in the result — read it with read_file (offset/limit) or grep rather than re-running the command.
Do not use a leading `sleep N` to wait for something: it blocks the agent loop and is rejected for N >= 2 seconds. Start long-running work with run_in_background=true and wait on it with shell_output({id, wait: "output"}) for its next write or wait: "exit" for its verdict; either wakes the moment the event lands. Do not call shell_output in a loop; that is what wait replaces. Use shell_tasks to list background task ids, and monitor_command when a watch should keep running and wake you on its own schedule.
It should be used when you need to run build or test commands, execute system utilities, interact with CLI tools, perform file operations that require shell commands, or integrate with external programs and scripts.
Important: Commands execute with the permissions of the current process. Be cautious with commands that modify the filesystem or system state. Always validate and sanitize any user-provided input before including it in commands.

command.description: The shell command to execute. Can be any valid shell command available in the system PATH or built-in shell commands. Common commands include: "npm" for Node.js packages, "git" for version control, "ls"/"dir" for listing files, "echo" for output, "cat"/"type" for file contents. The command string is passed to the system shell (sh on Unix, cmd.exe on Windows). Special characters should be properly escaped. Cannot be empty.

args.description: Optional array of arguments to pass to the command. Each argument is passed as a separate string and is automatically escaped for shell safety. Use this instead of including arguments in the command string for better security and cross-platform compatibility. Examples: ["install", "--save-dev", "typescript"] for npm, ["status", "--short"] for git, ["-la", "/usr"] for ls. Arguments containing spaces or special characters are automatically quoted.

cwd.description: Optional working directory where the command should be executed. Accepts absolute or relative paths; relative paths are resolved against the current working directory. The path must be inside the workspace (the current directory or one of its added directories) and must exist. Examples: "src" runs in src folder, "packages/core" runs in packages/core, "/Users/you/project/packages/core" runs in the specified absolute path. If omitted, uses the current working directory. Useful for running commands that depend on specific file locations or configurations.

timeout.description: Optional maximum time in milliseconds to wait for the command to complete before forcibly terminating it. Defaults to 30000ms (30 seconds); values above 600000 (10 minutes) are clamped to that maximum. The command process tree is killed if it exceeds this duration; any partial output captured so far is still returned. Set higher for operations known to take time (builds, installs), lower for quick operations. Examples: 5000 for quick commands, 60000 for npm install, 120000 for large builds. Pass 0 to disable the timeout entirely (prefer run_in_background=true for anything long-lived).

run_in_background.description: When true, start the command as a tracked background shell task and return immediately instead of waiting for completion. Use for dev servers, watchers, and long-running services. Output is captured to a task log file and the command can be listed with shell_tasks or stopped with kill_shell by taskId.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in 5-10 words, in active voice. Shown to the user while the command runs.

name: powershell
description:
Executes a PowerShell command on Windows with an optional timeout. The working directory persists between calls; variables and functions do not.

Use this tool for terminal programs, version control, package managers, containers, and PowerShell cmdlets. Use the dedicated tools for ordinary file work: glob for file search (not recursive Get-ChildItem), grep for content search (not Select-String), read_file (not Get-Content), edit_file / write_file (not Set-Content or Out-File). Respond in conversation directly, not with Write-Output or Write-Host.

PowerShell edition: resolved at run time (the result reports which executed). Until confirmed, use the Windows PowerShell 5.1-compatible subset:
- Do NOT use &&, ||, ternary, ?? or ?. operators.
- Conditional sequencing: A; if ($?) { B }. Unconditional sequencing: A; B.

The process runs with -NoProfile -NonInteractive:
- Never use Read-Host, Get-Credential, Out-GridView, host choice prompts, pause, interactive git modes, or commands that open an editor.
- Suppress intentional destructive confirmations explicitly with -Confirm:$false; use -Force only when its semantics are intended.

PowerShell syntax essentials:
- Variables use $; the escape character is the backtick, not backslash.
- Prefer full Verb-Noun cmdlet names over aliases (ls, cd, cat, rm are aliases of Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, Get-Content, Remove-Item).
- Pipelines pass objects; use Select-Object, Where-Object, Sort-Object to filter and shape.
- Double-quoted strings interpolate; single-quoted strings are literal.
- Environment variables read and assign via $env:NAME.
- Invoke a native executable whose path contains spaces with the call operator: & "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1.
- For multiline native arguments prefer a literal here-string (@' … '@); the closing '@ must start at column zero on its own line.
- Use the stop-parsing token --% when native arguments contain PowerShell metacharacters.

Usage:
- command is required.
- timeout is optional in milliseconds; defaults to 120000 and is capped at 600000.
- Provide a concise active-voice description of what the command does.
- Set run_in_background=true for dev servers, watchers, and long-running work; the call returns a task id inspectable via shell_tasks and stoppable via kill_shell. Never poll with Start-Sleep loops.
- Issue independent commands as separate parallel tool calls; chain dependent commands with the edition-appropriate syntax above. Semicolon is unconditional sequencing.
- Do not prepend cd/Set-Location merely to reach the already-selected project directory; pass cwd instead.
- Prefer a new commit over amending; consider safer alternatives before destructive git operations; never skip hooks or signing unless explicitly requested.

command.description: The PowerShell command to execute. Runs under -NoProfile -NonInteractive; never use interactive prompts (Read-Host, Get-Credential, pause). The working directory persists between calls; variables and functions do not.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 120000; capped at 600000. The process tree is terminated when exceeded.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in 5-10 words, in active voice. Shown to the user while the command runs.

cwd.description: Optional working directory for this command. Must be inside the workspace. Prefer this over prepending Set-Location.

run_in_background.description: When true, start the command as a tracked background task and return immediately with a task id. Use for dev servers, watchers, and long-running services; inspect with shell_tasks, stop with kill_shell.

name: activate_skill
description:
Load a skill's full instructions by name (progressive disclosure tier 2), optionally passing arguments.

WHEN TO CALL:
- The user's request matches a skill's <description> or trigger phrases in <available_skills>. A matching skill is BLOCKING: activate it before any other response about the task.
- Never mention a skill to the user without actually activating it.

ARGUMENTS:
- Pass everything the skill needs in "arguments" as one string — exactly what a user would type after "/name". Follow the skill's <argument-hint> when one is listed.

RULES:
- Do not re-activate a skill already loaded this turn (a <command-name> tag in the current context means it is loaded — follow it instead).
- The result lists the skill's bundled resource files; read them with the file tools only when the instructions call for them.

name.description: The skill name exactly as listed in <available_skills>.

arguments.description: Optional arguments for the skill, as a single string (what a user would type after "/name").

name: agent
description:
Delegate a task to a specialized sub-agent that runs autonomously and returns a single final result.
Choose the sub-agent whose purpose best matches the task and pass it a complete, self-contained prompt.
Launch independent tasks concurrently by emitting multiple task calls in one turn.
Set run_in_background: true for long tasks you do not need before continuing — collect results later with the agent_output tool.

Available agents (subagent_type):
- general: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions and executing multi-step tasks autonomously. The default when no specialized agent fits
- explore: Use this for codebase exploration, search, or understanding tasks that require multiple file operations
- plan: Use this to design implementation approaches by synthesizing exploration findings and considering architectural trade-offs

description.description: A short (3-5 word) label for this task, shown to the user while the sub-agent works.

subagent_type.description: Which sub-agent to run — pick the one whose purpose matches the task. Omit to use 'general'.

prompt.description: The full, self-contained task for the sub-agent. It runs autonomously in its own context and cannot ask follow-ups, so include every detail it needs and state exactly what to return.

model.description: Optional model override for this one run. Omit to use the agent's configured model (its frontmatter `model:`, else the session model). Only set this when the user explicitly asked for a specific model.

run_in_background.description: Run the sub-agent in the background and return immediately with an agent_id. Collect the result later with the agent_output tool.

name: agent_output
description: Retrieve results from background sub-agents launched with the agent tool. Default action 'wait' blocks until the agent finishes and returns its result; 'status' returns the current state immediately; 'kill' interrupts a running agent. Omit agent_id to list every background agent and its status.

agent_id.description: The agent_id returned when the task was launched. Omit to list all background agents.

action.description: What to do: 'wait' (default) blocks until completion and returns the result; 'status' peeks without blocking; 'kill' interrupts the agent.

name: search_tools
description: Load the full schema of a tool listed under "Additional tools" in your system prompt. Pass a short description of the capability you need, or select:<name> to load specific tools by name. Returns each match with its complete parameter schema; call the tool directly by its own name afterwards.

query.description: The capability you need, e.g. "schedule a recurring job". Or select:web_search,web_fetch for exact names.
